title: ASIC draws line in the sand on private credit
full_text:
The corporate regulator has put the under-pressure private credit sector on notice, warning it will add to regulation and take enforcement action if the industry doesn’t improve standards.
Speaking at an event in Sydney on Tuesday, Australian Securities & Investments Commissioner Simone Constant will say the regulator continues to see issues in private credit, including around valuations, liquidity, governance, conflicts and transparency.
Troubled Sydney developer Bathla Group, which called in administrators last month owing $3.4bn, underscores the need for strong governance, effective oversight, and accurate valuations, Ms Constant will say.
“The stress fractures we’re starting to see represent a line in the sand for private credit,” she will tell the Commercial & Asset Finance Brokers Association of Australia. “Private credit – done well – has an important role to play in driving Australia’s growth and productivity. But trust in the sector depends on high standards and best practice principles.” ASIC has been pushing the sector to lift its standards for more than a year, but Ms Constant will say the regulator is now beyond warnings. “The sector should prepare for enforcement action. We put it on notice in terms of 30 June valuations – but now we need to see practices lift across the board.
“Managers must provide complete clarity regarding borrower arrears, interest capitalisation, developer exposures, and the exact rules governing redemption queues,” Ms Constant will say.
Institutional investors, and superannuation trustees have a role to play too, according to the corporate cop.
“They can’t treat private credit as an easy, high-yielding substitute for traditional fixed-income investments while accepting manager marks at face value.
“Trustees have clear statutory obligations to act in their members’ best financial interests. Fulfilling that duty requires genuine, look-through due diligence.” Valuers, auditors and ratings agencies also have a crucial role to play, according to Ms Constant. “They need to ensure valuations reflect reality, risks are recognised early, and investors can have confidence that the information and the assessments they are relying on are sound.”
